human_readable: UN Security Council Resolution 242 — The Withdrawal Clause
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The fixed substrate is the withdrawal clause of UNSC Resolution 242 (adopted 22 Nov 1967), whose English text reads 'withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied' while the equally-authentic French text reads 'des territoires occupés.' Reading A (maximal withdrawal) treats the absent definite article as a translation accident and the French as controlling, grounding authority in the territorial-integrity norm of the Charter; structurally a Rope binding the occupying power to full retrocession, with beneficiaries being the dispossessed claimants. Reading B (partial withdrawal) treats the indefinite English as a deliberately negotiated ambiguity granting discretion over which territories, grounding authority in the drafters' intent and 'secure and recognized boundaries'; structurally a Ledger that converts indefiniteness into a bargaining asset, with the victim set being claimants left without a fixed line to enforce.

human_readable: Treaty of Waitangi — Māori and English Texts
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is the Treaty of Waitangi (6 Feb 1840), signed predominantly in a Māori text that cedes 'kāwanatanga' (governance) and guarantees chiefs 'tino rangatiratanga' (full chieftainship), against an English text ceding 'sovereignty.' Reading A (Crown-cession) reads the English as controlling and kāwanatanga as full sovereignty, grounding authority in the act of signature and subsequent settler statute; structurally a Wall enclosing land and lawmaking under the Crown, beneficiaries being the colonial state and settler purchasers. Reading B (rangatiratanga-retention) reads contra proferentem against the drafting Crown and treats the Māori text as controlling, so only limited governance was ceded; structurally a Rope of ongoing partnership and a Snare exposed in retrospect, with the victim set being hapū stripped of land and authority under a translation they could not have assented to.

human_readable: The Filioque Clause of the Nicene Creed
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381), whose article on the Spirit 'who proceeds from the Father' was unilaterally amended in the Latin West to 'from the Father and the Son' (Filioque). Reading A (Western, Filioque) treats the addition as a legitimate clarification, grounding authority in papal and conciliar competence to expound the deposit of faith; structurally an Anchor fixing doctrinal unity under a single magisterium, beneficiaries being the centralized Roman see. Reading B (Eastern, mono-procession) treats the unamended creed as inviolable and the unilateral edit as a breach of conciliar consent, grounding authority in the ecumenical council alone; structurally a Wall against any see legislating dogma for the whole Church, with the victim set being communions whose canonical autonomy is overridden — a divergence that helped fix the 1054 schism.

human_readable: The Second Amendment to the U.S. Constitution
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is the 27-word Second Amendment (ratified 1791): 'A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.' Reading A (individual right) treats the operative clause as primary and the militia preamble as non-limiting, grounding authority in the pre-existing right and originalist text (Heller, 2008); structurally a Wall protecting private possession against state restriction, beneficiaries being individual owners and the firearms market. Reading B (militia-conditioned) reads the prefatory clause as defining the right's scope, grounding authority in the collective-defense purpose and the regulatory power of the state; structurally a Lever for public arms governance, with the victim set being those exposed to harms that the individual-right reading treats as the price of an unconditioned entitlement.

human_readable: Outer Space Treaty Article II — Non-Appropriation
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is Article II of the Outer Space Treaty (1967): outer space and celestial bodies are 'not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means.' Reading A (extraction-permissive) holds that a bar on sovereign appropriation does not bar private ownership of extracted resources, grounding authority in the freedom-of-use clause and codifying it in domestic statute (U.S. 2015 Act, Luxembourg 2017); structurally a Ledger converting the commons into severable private title, beneficiaries being first-mover mining firms and their flag states. Reading B (commons-conservation) reads non-appropriation as covering use and occupation precisely to forestall de facto enclosure, grounding authority in the 'province of all mankind' and common-heritage norm; structurally a Wall around a shared commons, with the victim set being non-spacefaring states excluded from resources distributed by capability rather than by right.

human_readable: The GNU GPL — Linking and 'Derivative Work'
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is the GNU General Public License text (v2 1991, v3 2007) and its trigger phrase obligating disclosure for any 'work based on the Program.' Reading A (FSF, broad copyleft) holds that linking a program against GPL code — even dynamically — creates a derivative work, grounding authority in the license's intent to propagate freedom; structurally a Rope that pulls dependent code into the commons, beneficiaries being downstream users guaranteed source access. Reading B (narrow, linking-permissive) holds that mere linking does not create a derivative under copyright's idea/expression line, grounding authority in statutory copyright rather than license intent; structurally a Wall protecting proprietary modules that merely interface, with the victim set being users of those modules who lose the source-availability the broad reading would have secured — a contest largely unresolved by binding precedent.

KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is the 2008 Bitcoin whitepaper, 'A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System,' and its title-level claim about the network's purpose. Reading A (small-block / store-of-value) treats decentralization and full-node verifiability as the constraint the system exists to observe, so on-chain capacity must stay small and payments move to higher layers; structurally an Anchor prioritizing settlement assurance, beneficiaries being long-term holders and node operators. Reading B (big-block / electronic cash) treats the title's 'cash' as the binding telos, requiring large blocks and low on-chain fees for everyday payment; structurally a Lever for transactional throughput, with the victim set being low-value users priced off the base chain under Reading A — an incompatibility that crystallized in the 2017 Bitcoin Cash hard fork from a single unchanged founding text.

KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is Article 9 of the 1947 Japanese Constitution, renouncing war and stating that 'land, sea, and air forces, as well as other war potential, will never be maintained.' Reading A (strict pacifist) treats the text as a categorical bar on armed forces and on collective self-defense, grounding authority in the plain renunciation and postwar settlement; structurally a Wall enclosing the state's war-making capacity, beneficiaries being a population insulated from militarization and neighboring states historically harmed by it. Reading B (reinterpretation) treats an inherent right of self-defense as surviving, licensing Self-Defense Forces and, after the 2014 cabinet decision, limited collective self-defense, grounding authority in executive interpretation and security necessity; structurally a Lever expanding deployable force without textual amendment, with the victim set being the constitutional constraint itself and those relying on its fixity against incremental erosion.

human_readable: The Second Commandment and the Iconoclast Controversy
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is the Decalogue prohibition (Exodus 20:4) against making 'a graven image' or any likeness for worship, the fixed text contested in the Byzantine Iconoclasm (726–787, 814–843). Reading A (iconoclast) reads the prohibition as covering all religious imagery, equating veneration with idolatry, grounding authority in the literal command and imperial enforcement; structurally a Wall against material mediation of the holy, beneficiaries being a centralizing authority that monopolizes legitimate religious form. Reading B (iconodule) distinguishes worship (latria) owed to God from honor (dulia) passing through the image to its prototype, grounding authority in the Incarnation and tradition (Second Council of Nicaea, 787); structurally a Rope linking the faithful to the divine through sanctioned matter, with the victim set being communities, artisans, and devotional practices destroyed when the iconoclast reading prevails.

human_readable: The NPT — Peaceful Use vs. Disarmament Obligation
summary: KERNEL CONTEST: [ANALYTICAL ESTIMATE] The substrate is the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (1968/1970), whose Article IV affirms an 'inalienable right' to peaceful nuclear technology and whose Article VI obligates parties to pursue disarmament 'in good faith.' Reading A (non-proliferation-primary, often nuclear-weapon states) foregrounds Article IV's limits and verification while treating Article VI as aspirational, grounding authority in the security interest of preventing spread; structurally a Wall fixing a two-tier order, beneficiaries being existing weapon states whose arsenals face no enforceable deadline. Reading B (grand-bargain, often non-weapon states) reads Article VI as a binding reciprocal duty whose breach undermines Article IV's restraints, grounding authority in the treaty's bargained equality; structurally a Rope of mutual obligation, with the victim set being non-weapon states asked to forgo arms indefinitely against a disarmament promise the first reading renders unenforceable.
